newsitem.title: BRAZIL: FOCUS-Monster Brazil Oct trade gap prompts gloom.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Monster Brazil Oct trade gap prompts gloom.

text.p: Brazil's whopping $1.308 billion October trade deficit confirmed the most pessimistic projections for last month's trade balance and raised questions about how fast the country can afford to grow.
"This means trade is indeed deteriorating," said Marcelo Carvalho, chief economist at J.P. Morgan's Brazil unit.
"It raises questions about how fast Brazil can afford to grow without facing external controls, which will lead to the emergence of stop-and-go policies in the future. And that is not good."
The record monthly gap figure exceeded forecasts which had put it at between $900 million and $1 billion, mostly due to larger-than-expected oil imports last month.
Analysts said they have revised projections for the year-end trade deficit to between $4.5 billion and $5 billion, against 1995's $3.2 billion trade gap.
They said they expected the size of the deficit to shrink in November but increase once again in December.
The October results show imports are growing faster than the economy is expanding while exports remain sluggish, a recipe for tighter monetary policies, economists said.
Economists say playing with monetary policy, such as restricting credit, raising import tariffs and interest rates, will provide only short-term solutions, resulting in a "stop-and-go" growth policy.
"Instead of wasting energy and time tinkering with monetary policy, the government should seek vigorous export growth," said Mauro Schneider, chief economist for ING Barings in Brazil.

Markets remained calm after the Industry and Commerce Ministry released the figures as the worst-case-scenario had been factored into prices over recent days, especially after a major newspaper published a leaked $1.3 billion figure Thursday.
"It's bad news but its bad news the market has somehow digested," said Armando Goncalves, an economist with Brazil's Unibanco.
Government officials have repeatedly stated they are not concerned about the ballooning trade deficit but most analysts said they have no choice but to sound upbeat.
Predictably, Finance Ministry officials said the October trade numbers were no cause for alarm.

"What we think is there is no reason to change anything in the structure of macroeconomic policy," said Economic Policy secretary Jose Roberto Mendonca de Barros told reporters after the trade figures were announced.
